_meta.title: IS-IS Watcher bootcamp runbook - Topolograph
_meta.description: Run controlled IS-IS changes in the six-router isis01 lab and verify each one from the Watcher CSV through Topolograph Monitoring, the SDK, and the agent.

page_intro: Make one controlled change at a time, predict its effect, then verify the same fact from the Watcher event through Topolograph.

resources.label: IS-IS Watcher - repository and deploy guide

evidence_status_body: Every command below was run by hand against a freshly deployed isis01 lab. The Watcher CSV lines and SDK output are literal captures from that run (graph 07Sep2026_06h49m43s_6_hosts); the agent answer is one real Qwen response.
verify_intro: Open each source available in your environment and check it against the examples below.
agent_answer_label: Captured answer (Qwen; wording varies between runs)

sections.title: How this runbook works
paragraphs: For each exercise: make one change, predict the IS-IS result, observe the Watcher event, then find the same fact in Topolograph Monitoring, in the SDK, and - for the correlation exercise - in the agent's answer. Restore the lab before the next independent exercise.

isis01 is a six-router FRR domain in one area (`49.0001`, AS `65100`). `router2`-`router3` runs Level-1-2; `router3` to `router6` and `router3`'s leg to the `router4`/`router5` LAN are Level-2-only. The Watcher rides a Level-2 adjacency on `router1` and resolves each System ID to its hostname through the IS-IS dynamic-hostname TLV, so events name `router2`, `router3`, `router6` rather than `0100.1001.000x`.
steps: The Watcher CSV line is the deterministic source event.
Monitoring and the SDK prove the event was ingested and is queryable.
The agent is used only to correlate several events into one incident, never as a replacement for the source line.

sections.title: Bringing up the six-router lab
paragraphs: Run the public GRE-based isis01 topology from the IS-IS Watcher repository. `prepare.sh` also creates the `isis-br-dr` bridge and loads the MPLS kernel modules that IS-IS TE needs.

First check whether a lab is already running with `sudo clab inspect --all`. If a stale isis01 is listed, tear it down with `sudo clab destroy --topo isis01.clab.yml --cleanup` from `containerlab/isis01/` before deploying again - name the topology file so no other lab is touched.
sections.command:
cd containerlab/isis01
sudo clab inspect --all
sudo clab destroy --topo isis01.clab.yml --cleanup   # only if a stale isis01 is listed
sudo ./prepare.sh
sudo clab deploy --topo isis01.clab.yml
sudo docker logs clab-isis01-isis-watcher
sudo tail -f watcher/logs/watcher1.isis.log
observations: Six router containers plus the watcher are up: `docker ps --filter name=clab-isis01` lists `clab-isis01-router1..6` and `clab-isis01-isis-watcher`, all `State=Up`.
The watcher has the LSDB and is sniffing: `docker logs clab-isis01-isis-watcher` shows `ISIS LSDB has been received` and `Sniffing packets on interface: eth1`.
Adjacencies are Up: `docker exec clab-isis01-router1 vtysh -c 'show isis neighbor'` lists `router3` in the `Up` state; the first Topolograph graph then contains six routers.
sections.rollback: When you finish the runbook, remove the lab with `sudo clab destroy --topo isis01.clab.yml --cleanup` from `containerlab/isis01/`.

sections.title: Network event record format
paragraphs: The runbook uses three event families: `host`, `metric`, and `network`. Read `event_object` as the changed object, `event_status` as the transition, and `event_detected_by` as the advertising or detecting router. `graph_time` is the watcher's own label for the run and selects the Topolograph graph.

IS-IS lines carry a `level` field (`1` or `2`) that OSPF lines do not - it is the third field, right after `watcher_name`. Read the `metric` line above as one sentence: at `2026-09-07T06:55:14Z` the watcher `lab-isis01` saw `router3` re-advertise its Level-1 link toward `router2` with the metric changed from `10` to `-1` (adjacency lost), on the interface addressed `192.168.23.2` in area `49.0001` / AS `65100`. The identity behind `router2` is its NET / System ID `49.0001.0100.1001.0002.00`; the watcher prints the hostname because every router advertises the dynamic-hostname TLV.

A plain `host` or `network` up/down line carries no cost fields, so Fluent Bit forwards only the paired `changed` line. Topolograph reads an adjacency going down from the `metric` line whose `new_cost` is `-1`, and coming back from the one whose `old_cost` is `-1`.
steps: `area_num` `49.0001` and `asn` `65100` identify the routing domain; `sesid` is the watcher session, `srcid` the source router System ID (`router1`, `0100.1001.0001`).

sections.title: Where events come from
paragraphs: One IS-IS change produces one Watcher CSV line per level. Fluent Bit forwards it to Topolograph, which stores it and exposes it through the Monitoring page, the event API, and the SDK. Each exercise below checks the same fact at every level available to you.
steps: isis01 Watcher log  ->  Fluent Bit CSV parser  ->  Topolograph ingestion  ->  Monitoring page + event API  ->  Topolograph SDK

Monitoring page: OSPF/IS-IS Real-Time Monitoring. Pick the graph by its timestamp in `Choose the graph`, set the `From`/`To` window in UTC, turn on the `L1` and `L2` toggles, click `Find logs`; the `New/Old Subnets`, `Up/Down Links` and `Changed metric` toggles filter what is listed.
The graph selector lists every topology snapshot the watcher reported - that is the topology the watcher sent.
sections.image_alt: Topolograph OSPF/IS-IS Real-Time Monitoring controls for graph 07Sep2026_06h49m43s_6_hosts: the graph selector, the From/To time window, the L1 and L2 level toggles both on, the New/Old Subnets, Up/Down Links and Changed metric toggles, and Find logs. The Watchers Status panel reads "No watchers registered yet" because the containerlab watcher posts topology but not heartbeats.
sections.sdk_request:
from topolograph import Topolograph

topo = Topolograph(url="http://<your-topolograph>:8080",
                   username="<email>", password="<password>")
graph = topo.graphs.get(latest=True)
print(graph.graph_time, graph.protocol, graph.hosts)

sections.title: Cost change on a point-to-point link
paragraphs: Change `router2` `eth1` toward `router3`. IS-IS metrics are directed, so the reverse `router3`-to-`router2` metric must not be described as the same scalar. `router2` `eth1` has no explicit `isis metric`, so it starts at the wide-metric default of `10`. `router2`-`router3` is a Level-1-2 circuit, so the change is advertised at both levels.
sections.command:
sudo docker exec clab-isis01-router2 vtysh \
  -c 'conf t' -c 'interface eth1' -c 'isis metric 222'
sections.rollback: Run `isis metric 10` (or `no isis metric`) on `router2` `eth1` and confirm the inverse `222` -> `10` `metric` and `network` events.

verify.summary: The metric and network lines for the change and its rollback, at L1 and L2
The 10 -> 222 metric change on the event feed
verify.path: On OSPF/IS-IS Real-Time Monitoring, pick `07Sep2026_06h49m43s_6_hosts` in `Choose the graph`, set the `From`/`To` window around 06:52 UTC, turn on `L1` and `L2`, and click `Find logs`. With `Changed metric` on, the feed shows `object` `router3`, `detected by` `router2`, `10` -> `222` - the `router2` -> `router3` direction only, once for L1 and once for L2. The reverse direction is not listed.

verify.summary: get_adjacency_events and get_network_events return the same object and costs
verify.request:
adj = graph.events.get_adjacency_events(
    start_time="2026-09-07T06:52:14Z", end_time="2026-09-07T06:52:20Z")
net = graph.events.get_network_events(
    start_time="2026-09-07T06:52:14Z", end_time="2026-09-07T06:52:20Z")
for e in adj["adjacency_cost_change_events"]:
    print(e.event_object, e.event_detected_by, e.old_cost, "->", e.new_cost, "L" + str(e.level_number))
for e in net["network_cost_change_events"]:
    print(e.event_object, e.old_cost, "->", e.new_cost, "L" + str(e.level_number))
verify.note: The `metric` event names the `router2` -> `router3` direction (`event_object` `router3`, `event_detected_by` `router2`), `10` -> `222`, at both levels; the IPv4 and IPv6 connected subnets carry the same move. The reverse direction is absent.

verify.summary: A generic incident question about router2
verify.prompt: What happened with router2 in the last 10 minutes?
verify.note: A passing answer names the `router2` -> `router3` direction and both metric values (`10` and `222`) without the question naming cost or metric, and does not claim the reverse `router3` -> `router2` direction changed.

sections.title: Detecting internal and external prefix events
paragraphs: Run each prefix experiment independently. Unlike OSPF, IS-IS advertises a loopback with the mask it is configured with and costs it at the interface metric - a `/24` stays a `/24` at cost `10`, it is not collapsed to a `/32` host route. `router6` is Level-2-only, so its prefixes appear at L2 alone.
steps: 6a. On `router2`, `interface lo` / `ip address 192.168.123.1/24`; observe `192.168.123.0/24` up and cost `-1` -> `10` at L1 and L2.
6b. On `router6`, `interface lo` / `ip address 10.10.36.6/24`; observe `10.10.36.0/24` up and cost `-1` -> `10` at L2.

6c. On `router6`, `no ip route 6.6.6.6/32 192.168.36.3`; observe `6.6.6.6/32` down and cost `11` -> `-1` at L2. FRR redistributes it into IS-IS without the external bit, so the watcher tags it `internal`.
sections.command:
sudo docker exec clab-isis01-router2 vtysh \
  -c 'conf t' -c 'interface lo' -c 'ip address 192.168.123.1/24'
sections.rollback: 6a: `no ip address 192.168.123.1/24` on `router2` `interface lo`. 6b: `no ip address 10.10.36.6/24` on `router6` `interface lo`. 6c: `ip route 6.6.6.6/32 192.168.36.3` on `router6`. Confirm the inverse event after each.

verify.summary: One up/down and one changed line per sub-exercise
The new and withdrawn prefixes on the feed
verify.path: On OSPF/IS-IS Real-Time Monitoring, pick this graph, set the window around 06:52-06:55 UTC, turn on `L1` and `L2`, and click `Find logs`. With `New/Old Subnets` on, `192.168.123.0/24` and `10.10.36.0/24` appear as added and `6.6.6.6/32` as withdrawn.

verify.summary: get_network_events, one changed event per sub-exercise
verify.request:
for start, end in [("2026-09-07T06:52:50Z", "2026-09-07T06:52:55Z"),
                   ("2026-09-07T06:53:37Z", "2026-09-07T06:53:42Z"),
                   ("2026-09-07T06:54:12Z", "2026-09-07T06:54:17Z")]:
    net = graph.events.get_network_events(start_time=start, end_time=end)
    for e in net["network_up_down_events"]:
        print(e.event_object, e.event_status, e.event_detected_by,
              f"{e.old_cost} -> {e.new_cost}", "L" + str(e.level_number), e.subnet_type)
verify.output:
192.168.123.0/24 changed router2 -1 -> 10 L1 internal
192.168.123.0/24 changed router2 -1 -> 10 L2 internal
10.10.36.0/24 changed router6 -1 -> 10 L2 internal
6.6.6.6/32 changed router6 11 -> -1 L2 internal
verify.note: The `/24` keeps its mask - no `/32` collapse. Availability is an up/down line the forwarder drops; the cost move is the `changed` event the SDK returns. `router2`'s loopback is seen at L1 and L2, `router6`'s only at L2, and the redistributed `6.6.6.6/32` is tagged `internal`.

sections.title: Detecting a connectivity loss and its recovery
paragraphs: Shut `router2` `eth1`, inspect the correlated event set, then restore the interface with `no shutdown`. Because `router2`-`router3` is Level-1-2, every line appears once for L1 and once for L2.
sections.command:
# down
sudo docker exec clab-isis01-router2 vtysh \
  -c 'conf t' -c 'interface eth1' -c 'shutdown'
# recovery
sudo docker exec clab-isis01-router2 vtysh \
  -c 'conf t' -c 'interface eth1' -c 'no shutdown'
sections.rollback: `no shutdown` on `router2` `eth1` restores the interface; wait for the `host`, `network` and `metric` recovery events at both levels.

verify.summary: The L1 down set and the L1 recovery set for the router2-router3 link
The outage as one wave on the feed
verify.path: On OSPF/IS-IS Real-Time Monitoring, pick this graph, set the window around 06:55 UTC, turn on `L1` and `L2`, and click `Find logs`. With `Up/Down Links` on, `router2` and `router3` each show their side of the link going to `-1` and back, and `192.168.23.0/24` goes unreachable and returns - twice, once per level.

verify.summary: get_adjacency_events returns the paired down/up moves
verify.request:
down = graph.events.get_adjacency_events(
    start_time="2026-09-07T06:55:14Z", end_time="2026-09-07T06:55:16Z")
for e in down["all_host_up_down_events"]:
    print(e.event_object, "detected_by", e.event_detected_by,
          f"{e.old_cost} -> {e.new_cost}", "L" + str(e.level_number))
verify.output:
router2 detected_by router3 10 -> -1 L1
router3 detected_by router2 10 -> -1 L1
router2 detected_by router3 10 -> -1 L2
router3 detected_by router2 10 -> -1 L2
verify.note: `host` `router2` down detected by `router3`, both directed metrics to `-1`, `192.168.23.0/24` down - at L1 and L2; then the mirror recovery. On recovery the watcher also logs a `node` `attr:attached` flap on `router2`, which Topolograph does not yet ingest.

verify.summary: A generic incident question about the network
verify.prompt: What happened in the network in the last 30 minutes?
answer: In the last 30 minutes the IS-IS domain (area 49.0001, AS 65100) had 7 event waves detected by watcher lab-isis01, starting at 06:55:15 UTC. Every device that went down recovered within the window.
06:55:15 - router2 and router3 each lost the adjacency between them, at L1 and L2 (router2 detected by router3, router3 detected by router2).
06:55:40 - both routers restored that adjacency at L1 and L2, followed by a few repeated up notifications through 06:56:33.
06:57:23 - router6 lost its L2 adjacency to router3; 06:57:56 - router6 and router3 restored it.
In short: the router2-router3 link dropped at 06:55:15 and came back at 06:55:40; the router3-router6 link dropped at 06:57:23 and recovered at 06:57:56 - both fully converged.
verify.note: The answer names the failed adjacency (`router2` - `router3`), that `router3` detected `router2`'s loss and vice versa, both metrics at `-1`, and the recovery - the same facts as the CSV lines above, from a question that never says "adjacency" or "failure". The `router6` lines are the transit exercise below, caught by the same 30-minute window.

sections.title: Reporting on a broadcast transit segment
paragraphs: `router6` `eth1` faces `router3` on a broadcast (LAN) circuit. `router6` carries `isis priority 100` against `router3`'s `64`, so `router6` is the DIS and originates the pseudonode LSP. The circuit is Level-2-only, so every line is L2. `router6` `eth1` has no explicit `isis metric`, so the baseline is the default `10`.
sections.command:
# cost
sudo docker exec clab-isis01-router6 vtysh \
  -c 'conf t' -c 'interface eth1' -c 'isis metric 66'
# then, separately: shutdown, then no shutdown
sudo docker exec clab-isis01-router6 vtysh \
  -c 'conf t' -c 'interface eth1' -c 'shutdown'
sudo docker exec clab-isis01-router6 vtysh \
  -c 'conf t' -c 'interface eth1' -c 'no shutdown'
sections.rollback: `isis metric 10` (or `no isis metric`) on `router6` `eth1` restores the baseline `10`; `no shutdown` restores the adjacency. Confirm the inverse `metric` events.

verify.summary: The L2 cost change with its network side-effects, plus the shutdown/recovery pair
The transit cost change and the router6 outage, L2 only
verify.path: On OSPF/IS-IS Real-Time Monitoring, pick this graph, set the window around 06:56-06:58 UTC, turn on `L2`, and click `Find logs`. The `metric` event `object` is `router3` with `event_detected_by` `router6`, and the change is L2 only - the circuit is level-2-only. On shutdown the feed shows `host` `router6` down and `192.168.36.0/24` unreachable, then the recovery.

verify.summary: get_adjacency_events for the transit cost and the shutdown/recovery
verify.request:
cost = graph.events.get_adjacency_events(
    start_time="2026-09-07T06:56:46Z", end_time="2026-09-07T06:56:49Z")
for e in cost["adjacency_cost_change_events"]:
    print("cost", e.event_object, e.event_detected_by, f"{e.old_cost} -> {e.new_cost}", "L" + str(e.level_number))
flap = graph.events.get_adjacency_events(
    start_time="2026-09-07T06:57:21Z", end_time="2026-09-07T06:58:00Z")
for e in flap["all_host_up_down_events"]:
    print("updown", e.event_object, e.event_detected_by, f"{e.old_cost} -> {e.new_cost}", "L" + str(e.level_number))
verify.output:
cost router3 router6 10 -> 66 L2
updown router6 router3 10 -> -1 L2
updown router6 router3 -1 -> 10 L2
updown router3 router6 -1 -> 10 L2
verify.note: On the broadcast segment the `metric` event still names the neighbour (`router3`), detected by `router6`, and only at L2; the metric change also moves `192.168.36.0/24` and the two IPv6 `/127`s. The shutdown is `host` `router6` down at L2, then recovery.

verify.summary: A generic incident question about router6
verify.prompt: What happened on router6 in the last 20 minutes?
verify.note: A passing answer names the `router6` -> `router3` transit metric moving `10` -> `66` and back, then the `router6` attachment going down (metric `-1` at L2) and recovering, without the question naming cost, DIS, or shutdown.

sections.title: Changing a link's TE attributes
paragraphs: `router2` `eth1` toward `router3` already carries RFC 5305 TE sub-TLVs: `mpls-te on` plus per-interface `link-params` advertise Administrative Group, Maximum (Reservable) Bandwidth, and per-priority Unreserved Bandwidth alongside the ordinary metric. Changing one of those without touching the IGP metric still produces its own event family, `temetric`, distinct from `metric` -- and it fires once per level on this Level-1-2 circuit, same as `metric` does.

`admin-grp` is the field IS-IS/MPLS-TE uses for CSPF constraint-based routing ("avoid links outside the gold class"). `0x647a0001` sets bits `0,17,19,20,21,22,26,29,30`; the change below clears bit `0` and sets bit `1`, leaving every other bit untouched.
sections.command:
sudo docker exec clab-isis01-router2 vtysh \
  -c 'conf t' -c 'interface eth1' -c 'link-params' \
  -c 'admin-grp 0x647a0002'
sections.rollback: Run `admin-grp 0x647a0001` under `link-params` on `router2` `eth1` and confirm the inverse `temetric` events at L1 and L2.

verify.summary: The temetric events for the change and its rollback, at L1 and L2
The temetric row on the event feed
verify.path: On OSPF/IS-IS Real-Time Monitoring, pick `12Sep2026_19h04m47s_6_hosts` in `Choose the graph`, set the `From`/`To` window around 19:26 UTC, turn on `L1` and `L2`, and click `Find logs`. The change appears as a `temetric` row for `router3` detected by `router2`, at both levels.

verify.summary: get_adjacency_events returns the temetric change, correlated to the link and timestamp
verify.request:
adj = graph.events.get_adjacency_events(
    start_time="2026-09-12T19:26:18Z", end_time="2026-09-12T19:26:21Z")
for e in adj["adjacency_cost_change_events"]:
    print(e.event_name, e.event_object, e.event_detected_by, "L" + str(e.level_number))
verify.output:
temetric router3 router2 L1
temetric router3 router2 L2
verify.note: The SDK confirms a `temetric` change on this link at both levels, correlated to the same timestamp as the Watcher lines above -- but `get_adjacency_events` does not yet surface the changed admin-group, bandwidth or TE-metric values themselves; read those from the Watcher CSV or the `temetric_change` collection directly.

sections.title: Reading TE attributes and filtering edges by IS-IS level
paragraphs: Every parsed link carries its metric and RFC 5305 TE sub-TLVs (admin group, bandwidth pools, TE metric) alongside `isis_level` -- `1` or `2` for a link advertised at one level only, `3` (L1L2) for one advertised at both. `router3`-`router6` is Level-2-only, so it is the one edge on this graph tagged `isis_level: 2`; every other link here is `3`.

This graph (`18Sep2026_08h50m15s_6_hosts`) came from a full LSDB parse (`POST /graphs` with `router1`'s `show isis database detail`). A Watcher-sourced graph stores per-level TE snapshots the same way, so it answers a level-aware request with real data too.
sections.image_alt: The Web edge tooltip for router2-router3, now split into two side-by-side panels -- 0100.1001.0003 to 0100.1001.0002 (Metric 10) on the left and 0100.1001.0002 to 0100.1001.0003 (Metric 50) on the right -- each with its own Local/Remote IP, TE Metric, Bandwidth and Unreserved BW badges, plus the L1/L2 breakdown further down. Before the router2 mpls-te router-address fix (Point-to-point link section rollback note), router2's directed edges landed on two different vertices and this same link showed a single column with one direction missing.
observations: `isis_level=2` lists exactly one edge per direction on the Level-2-only circuit: `10.10.10.3 -> 10.10.10.6` and `10.10.10.6 -> 10.10.10.3`, both `isis_level: 2` -- no other link in this six-router graph matches.

`admin_group=0x647a0001` lists 2 edges: `10.10.10.1 -> 10.10.10.3` (cost 10) and `10.10.10.2 -> 10.10.10.3` (cost 50) -- the two directions `router1`/`router2` advertise toward `router3` with that group, each carrying its own `admin_group`, `temetric` and `unreserved_bw_0`..`unreserved_bw_7` fields.

`temetric__gt=25` lists 2 edges: `10.10.10.1 -> 10.10.10.3` (`temetric: 111111`) and `10.10.10.3 -> 10.10.10.2` (`temetric: 32`) -- the range operator reads the same TE-metric field the Web tooltip's `TE Metric` badge shows.

sections.title: Computing CSPF for one IS-IS level
paragraphs: `GET /graph/{graph_time}/cspf-path/{node_a}/{node_b}?level=1|2` answers a question the combined/default calculation cannot: which path, if any, exists using strictly that level's own advertised metrics and TE data. `router3`-`router6` is Level-2-only, so `router6` is not even a member of the Level-1 topology -- a Level-1 request between `router1` and `router6` is not a strict-constraint failure, it is `src/dst not found`.

Requesting an explicit `level` against a graph that predates per-level storage -- such as one uploaded before per-level snapshots were introduced -- fails closed with `422` and `code: isis_level_calculation_unavailable` rather than silently answering from the merged view.
observations: `level=1`: `"path": []`, `"reason": "src/dst not found"` -- `router6` has no Level-1 membership at all, on this or any graph, since its only circuit is Level-2-only.
`level=2`: identical to the combined view here (`"cost": 20`) -- this graph's one Level-1-2 hop, `router1`-`router3`, also advertises at L2, so the L2-only path matches the default one.

The same request against the pre-per-level graph `12Sep2026_19h04m47s_6_hosts` (`?level=1`) returns `422` with `"code": "isis_level_calculation_unavailable"`, `"action": "reupload_graph"` -- re-run the LSDB upload under the current Topolograph version to get a real per-level answer instead.

sections.title: Load the 13-router IS-IS lab
paragraphs: Situation: the six-router lab is enough to inspect Watcher events and TE fields, but it has no useful alternative routes for CSPF. There is no current 13-router CSPF route yet.

Task: deploy the `13-hosts-demo-isis` lab, capture the LSDB from `r30`, and upload it. Path computation needs alternative paths, so these steps use the same lab as the public Topolograph demo graph: [Topolograph](https://topolograph.com) and the [`13-hosts-demo-isis` lab](https://github.com/Vadims06/topolograph/tree/master/containerlab/13-hosts-demo-isis).
Result: the graph has 13 nodes and 52 directed edges: 12 Level-1 edges and 40 Level-2 edges. Fifty edges are TE links; the two directions of `r110-r111` are not TE links.
sections.command:
cd containerlab/13-hosts-demo-isis
sudo clab deploy --topo 13-hosts-demo-isis.clab.yml
sudo docker exec clab-13-hosts-demo-isis-r30 vtysh -c 'show isis database detail'
observations: The uploaded graph reports `{'count': 13}` hosts and 52 edges.
`edges_list(is_te_link=True)` returns 50 edges; `edges_list(is_te_link=False)` returns the two `r110`-`r111` directions.
sections.sdk_request:
from topolograph import Topolograph

topo = Topolograph(url="http://<your-topolograph>:8080", username="<email>", password="<password>")
graph = topo.graphs.upload(open("demo_isis_LSDB.txt").read(), vendor="FRR", protocol="isis")
print(graph.graph_time, graph.hosts)
print(graph.edges_list(per_page=200)["pagination"]["total"])
print(graph.edges_list(is_te_link=True, per_page=200)["pagination"]["total"])
print(graph.edges_list(is_te_link=False, per_page=200)["pagination"]["total"])

sections.title: Read TE values before computing a path
paragraphs: Situation: the current route is not constrained yet; the graph exposes TE attributes but a plain path calculation would not tell you which links are safe for a tunnel.
Task: identify gold and red admin groups, high TE metrics, the low priority-7 bandwidth pool, SRLG-bearing links, and links that are not TE-enabled before choosing a constraint.

Result: gold (`0x00000002`) returns 10 directed edges, red (`0x00000004`) returns 2, `temetric__gt=30` returns 4, `unreserved_bw_7__lt=1000000` returns 2, and `is_te_link=False` returns the 2 `r110-r111` edges.
sections.command: # Run from the SDK against the graph uploaded in step 1
observations: The 8 edges on `r10-r100` and `r100-r110`/`r100-r111` carry SRLG data; the two parallel `r10-r100` links keep their separate groups.
Passing `is_te_link='yes'` is rejected with HTTP 400: `Wrong type, expected 'boolean'`.
sections.sdk_request:
for query in (
    {'admin_group': '0x00000002'},
    {'admin_group': '0x00000004'},
    {'temetric__gt': 30},
    {'unreserved_bw_7__lt': 1_000_000},
    {'is_te_link': False},
):
    result = graph.edges_list(per_page=200, **query)
    print(query, result['pagination']['total'])

sections.title: Record the unconstrained route
paragraphs: Situation: `r10` to `r14` has no CSPF constraint, and the current shortest route is `r10 r100 r110 r14` with cost 30.
Task: save this route as the baseline so every following exercise can explain what changed and why.
Result: the reference route remains `r10 r100 r110 r14`, cost 30, using the `eth2` parallel link between `r10` and `r100`.
sections.command: # No router change: calculate the reference CSPF path
observations: The baseline uses IGP metrics. The next four steps deliberately move it with one constraint at a time.

sections.title: Avoid shared-risk groups
paragraphs: Situation: the current route is `r10 r100 r110 r14`, cost 30, and its first hop uses SRLG 300; both parallel first hops share SRLG 100.
Task: rebuild the route around the duct or link being serviced by applying `srlg_exclude`.

Result: excluding 300 keeps the routers but selects `eth1`, cost 35; excluding 100 gives `r10 r11 r100 r110 r14`, cost 40; excluding 200 gives `r10 r100 r101 r111 r14`, cost 45; excluding both 100 and 200 gives `r10 r11 r101 r111 r14`, cost 50.
sections.command: # No router change: change the excluded risk group in each request
observations: The route changes because the constraint removes links, not because any IGP metric changed.
sections.sdk_request:
for groups in ([300], [100], [200], [100, 200]):
    print(groups, graph.cspf_path('r10', 'r14', srlg_exclude=groups))

sections.title: Select a route by bandwidth and setup priority
paragraphs: Situation: the current route is `r10 r100 r110 r14`, cost 30, but `r100-r110` advertises only 4 Mbit in its priority-7 pool and 10 Mbit in priorities 0-3.
Task: place an 8 Mbit tunnel at different setup priorities, then test a 20 Mbit request that cannot fit anywhere.
Result: priority 7 moves the tunnel to `r10 r100 r111 r14`, cost 40; priority 0 keeps `r10 r100 r110 r14`, cost 30; 20 Mbit returns no path and a constraint refusal.
sections.command: # No router change: vary bandwidth and setup_priority
observations: Setup priority selects the advertised unreserved-bandwidth pool used for placement; it does not alter the route's IGP cost.

sections.title: Compute with the TE metric
paragraphs: Situation: the IGP route is `r10 r100 r110 r14`, cost 30; `r100-r110` has TE metric 100 while `r100-r111` has TE metric 10.
Task: rebuild the route using `metric_type='te'`, and verify that every link on the candidate route carries a TE metric.
Result: the TE route is `r10 r100 r111 r14`, TE cost 30. Its IGP cost is 40, so the selected metric is visible in the result.
sections.command: # No router change: select TE cost instead of IGP cost
observations: If a candidate link has no TE metric, CSPF falls back to IGP for that calculation; inspect the edge attributes first.

sections.title: Include or exclude admin-group bits
paragraphs: Situation: `r13` to `r15` currently costs 30 over `r13 r100 r110 r15`; admin-group bit 1 is gold and bit 2 is red.
Task: require gold links with `admin_include_all=['1']`, then avoid red links with `admin_exclude_any=['2']`.
Result: gold-only changes the route to `r13 r101 r111 r15`, cost 45; from `r10` to `r14`, gold-only gives `r10 r101 r111 r14`, cost 55; avoiding red gives `r13 r100 r111 r15`, cost 40.
sections.command: # No router change: admin groups are bit numbers, not hexadecimal mask values
observations: Bit 1 means mask `0x00000002`; bit 2 means mask `0x00000004`. Bit 0 is the least significant bit.
sections.sdk_request:
print(graph.cspf_path('r13', 'r15', admin_include_all=['1']))
print(graph.cspf_path('r10', 'r14', admin_include_all=['1']))
print(graph.cspf_path('r13', 'r15', admin_exclude_any=['2']))

sections.title: Restrict CSPF to one IS-IS level
paragraphs: Situation: `r30` to `r31` costs 10 on the direct Level-1 route, while the Level-2 route is `r30 r10 r11 r31`, cost 40.
Task: signal the tunnel in Level 2 with `level=2`, and check which endpoints exist in each independent topology.

Result: `r30` to `r31` is cost 10 at Level 1 and cost 40 at Level 2. `r130` to `r131` is cost 10 at Level 1 and `src/dst not found` at Level 2. `r130` to `r15` has combined cost 50 but no path at either single level because it would cross the level boundary.
sections.command: # No router change: constrain the request to Level 1 or Level 2
observations: An explicit level request on a graph stored before per-level data returns HTTP 422 with `code: isis_level_calculation_unavailable`; it must be reuploaded.

sections.title: Distinguish an unsatisfied constraint from a missing endpoint
paragraphs: Situation: the 20 Mbit request from step 5 has known endpoints but no link with enough bandwidth; the Level-1 `r130` to `r15` request has no common level containing both endpoints.
Task: read `reason` instead of treating every empty path as the same failure.
Result: the bandwidth request says `no path satisfies the requested constraints`; the wrong-level request says `src/dst not found`.
sections.command: # Repeat the failed requests from steps 5 and 8
observations: The first reason calls for relaxing bandwidth, affinity, or SRLG constraints; the second means the requested topology does not contain both endpoints.
sections.sdk_output:
{'cost': None, 'path': [], 'reason': 'no path satisfies the requested constraints'}
{'cost': None, 'path': [], 'reason': 'src/dst not found'}

sections.title: Edit one edge and recompute
paragraphs: Situation: the current route is `r10 r100 r110 r14`, cost 30. Maintenance is planned for `r100-r110`, but the router configuration must not change.
Task: use `update_edge` on a graph copy, add SRLG 999 to the Level-2 edge, recompute while excluding it, then clear the SRLG.

Result: excluding 999 changes the route to `r10 r100 r111 r14`, cost 40; clearing the SRLG restores `r10 r100 r110 r14`, cost 30. A Level-2-only edge rejects `isis_level=1`, and `replace_edge` removes per-level data so explicit-level CSPF returns 422.
sections.command:
# Run this on a disposable graph: the edit is persistent
# Find the edge id first with edges_list(include=['edge_key'])
observations: `update_edge` is partial; `replace_edge` is a full rewrite. Do not use either on the reference graph you want to keep unchanged.
sections.sdk_request:
edge = next(e for e in graph.edges_list(include=['edge_key'], per_page=200)['items']
             if e['src'] == 'r100' and e['dst'] == 'r110')
print(graph.update_edge(edge['id'], isis_level=2, srlg=[999]))
print(graph.cspf_path('r10', 'r14', srlg_exclude=[999]))
print(graph.update_edge(edge['id'], isis_level=2, srlg=[]))
print(graph.cspf_path('r10', 'r14'))

sections.title: Place tunnels and inspect residual bandwidth
paragraphs: Situation: no tunnel is placed, so the reference route is `r10 r100 r110 r14`, cost 30, and its 4 Mbit priority-7 pool is available.
Task: add four 4 Mbit tunnels from `r10` to `r14`, one at a time, and inspect residual bandwidth and the selected path after each placement.

Result: `T1` uses `r10 r100 r110 r14`, cost 30; `T2` uses `r10 r100 r111 r14`, cost 40; `T3` uses the other `r10-r100` link, cost 45; `T4` uses `r10 r11 r101 r110 r14`, cost 55. Delete all test LSPs afterwards.
sections.command: # No router change: create four 4 Mbit RSVP-TE tunnels through the SDK
observations: Use `edges_list(include=['lsp_left_bw', 'lsps'])` after each placement to see which pool caused the next route move.
Always call `delete_lsps()` in cleanup; LSP placement changes the stored graph.
